_meta.purpose: Hand-computed known-answer fixtures for financial and ML metric functions. Every 'expected' value here is derived by hand or from a closed-form/textbook source so the repo's own functions can be diffed against a ground truth. Do not 'fix' an expected value to make a test pass; a failing test means the code diverges from the stated convention.
_meta.tolerance_notes: abs_tol is an absolute tolerance on the metric value. Use the metric's own abs_tol; fall back to 1e-6 if a fixture omits it. Convention-sensitive metrics (Sharpe, VaR) list the exact convention the expected value assumes so a mismatch can be diagnosed as a convention bug rather than a math bug.

conventions_glossary.ddof: delta degrees of freedom for standard deviation. ddof=0 is population (numpy default), ddof=1 is sample (pandas .std() default). Sharpe/Sortino/vol change with this choice.
conventions_glossary.annualization: sqrt(252) for daily equity vol/Sharpe, sqrt(12) for monthly, sqrt(365) or sqrt(8760) for daily/hourly crypto. Annualizing the mean uses the factor itself (252), annualizing vol uses its sqrt.
conventions_glossary.return_type: simple = P_t/P_{t-1} - 1; log = ln(P_t/P_{t-1}). Sums and drawdowns differ between the two.
conventions_glossary.var_sign: loss-positive: VaR reported as a positive loss magnitude. return-negative: VaR reported as the negative return quantile. Both are 'right' but must be consistent and documented.
conventions_glossary.var_method: historical = empirical quantile of realized returns; parametric-normal = mu + z_alpha * sigma with z_0.95 = 1.645, z_0.99 = 2.326.

financial.convention: excess-return mean / std(ddof=1), risk_free=0, annualized by sqrt(252)
financial.derivation: mean=0.0035; sample std(ddof=1)=0.0124309; per-period Sharpe=0.281554; *sqrt(252)=15.874987 -> 4.469. NOTE: expected recomputed below in fixture note; use harness echo of observed and compare shape, not blind trust.
financial.recompute_note: mean(r)=0.0035, std(r,ddof=1)=0.012431 -> daily Sharpe 0.28155 -> annualized 0.28155*sqrt(252)=4.4695. If your function returns ~4.47 it uses ddof=1+sqrt(252). If ~4.71 it uses ddof=0. If ~0.28 it did not annualize.

financial.convention: mean / std(ddof=0) annualized by sqrt(252), risk_free=0
financial.recompute_note: std(r,ddof=0)=0.011792 -> daily Sharpe 0.296816 -> *sqrt(252)=4.7113. Distinguishes ddof=0 from ddof=1 (4.47).

financial.convention: mean / downside_deviation, downside dev uses returns below 0 (MAR=0), squared over N (population), annualized sqrt(252)
financial.recompute_note: downside returns squared: (-0.02)^2+(-0.01)^2+(-0.005)^2 = 0.0004+0.0001+0.000025 = 0.000525; /10 = 0.0000525; sqrt=0.0072457 downside dev. daily Sortino=0.0035/0.0072457=0.483 -> *sqrt(252)=7.669. If code divides downside sum by count-of-downside(3) instead of N(10): dd=sqrt(0.000525/3)=0.013229 -> 0.2646 -> *sqrt(252)=4.201. Report which denominator the code uses.

financial.convention: min over time of (equity/running_max - 1); reported as negative fraction. Input is an equity/price curve.
financial.recompute_note: running max at index of price 80 is 130; 80/130 - 1 = -0.384615. Deepest trough. If code returns +0.384615 it uses loss-positive sign. If it computes drawdown on returns not prices the answer will differ.

financial.convention: max drawdown of the equity curve built from simple returns via cumprod(1+r); reported as negative fraction
financial.recompute_note: cumprod(1+r) reproduces the price path 100->110->105->120->90->95->130->80->140 (scaled). Same trough 80 vs peak 130 -> -0.384615. Use to confirm the code builds the equity curve before measuring drawdown, not on raw returns.

financial.convention: parametric-normal 95% VaR = -(mu + z * sigma) with z_0.95 = -1.6448536; loss-positive; standard normal input (mu=0, sigma=1)
financial.recompute_note: For X ~ N(0,1), the 5th percentile is -1.6448536, so 95% VaR (loss-positive) = 1.6449. This is the canonical closed-form anchor. If code returns -1.6449 it uses return-negative sign; if ~1.645 loss-positive. If it uses z=1.65 rounded, tolerance covers it.

financial.convention: parametric-normal 95% CVaR (expected shortfall) = sigma * phi(z_alpha)/(1-alpha); standard normal; loss-positive
financial.recompute_note: CVaR_95 for N(0,1) = phi(1.6449)/(0.05) = 0.103135/0.05 = 2.06271. Canonical anchor. CVaR must always exceed VaR (2.063 > 1.645); if code returns CVaR < VaR the sign or averaging is wrong.

financial.convention: historical 95% VaR = negative of the empirical 5th-percentile return; loss-positive. Interpolation method matters near small samples.
financial.recompute_note: 20 sorted returns; 5th percentile lands between -0.10 and -0.08. numpy linear interpolation gives -0.081 -> loss-positive VaR 0.081. numpy 'lower' method gives -0.10 -> 0.10. Report which quantile interpolation the code uses; the gap (0.081 vs 0.10) is the whole point.
std(ddof=1)=0.012431 -> *sqrt(252)=0.19733. With ddof=0: 0.011792*sqrt(252)=0.18720. Distinguishes the ddof choice on vol.

ml.convention: area under ROC curve; 1.0 for a perfectly separating score
ml.recompute_note: All positives score above all negatives -> AUC exactly 1.0. If code returns 0.0 it likely inverted y_true/y_score arg order.

ml.convention: area under ROC curve, Mann-Whitney U formulation; handles ties by averaging
ml.recompute_note: Pairs (pos,neg): (0.35 vs 0.1)=win, (0.35 vs 0.4)=loss, (0.8 vs 0.1)=win, (0.8 vs 0.4)=win -> 3/4 = 0.75. Canonical sklearn example. If code returns 0.25 the labels/scores are swapped.

ml.convention: AUC of a constant score is 0.5 (no discrimination)
ml.recompute_note: All scores tied -> ROC is the diagonal -> 0.5. If code returns 0.0 or 1.0 it mishandles ties.

ml.convention: mean squared error between predicted probability and binary outcome; lower is better; 0 is perfect
Brier score is 0 when probabilities exactly match outcomes
ml.recompute_note: Perfect calibration and separation -> 0. Anchors the sign/scale.

ml.convention: binary cross-entropy, mean over samples, natural log, clipped to avoid log(0)
fraction of correct predictions; threshold 0.5 if scores are probabilities and function thresholds internally, else exact-match of labels
ml.recompute_note: 4 of 5 correct = 0.8. Use only when the function takes hard labels; if it takes probabilities it needs a threshold first.

ml.convention: expected calibration error with fixed equal-width bins over [0,1]; weighted average of |accuracy - confidence| per bin
ml.recompute_note: Bin1 [0,0.5): probs 0.2,0.3 conf=0.25 acc=0 -> |0.25-0|=0.25, weight 2/6. Bin2 [0.5,1]: probs 0.6..0.9 conf=0.75 acc=1 -> |0.75-1|=0.25, weight 4/6. ECE = (2/6)*0.25 + (4/6)*0.25 = 0.25. Binning edges/count are convention-sensitive; report n_bins and edge policy the code uses.
